rendered:
Yes. The counts agree, as long as you compare the text with the right study's bars in Fig. 2[1]E. The text says a pan-genome analysis of 45[2] isolates found "19,469 total genes, of which only 3155 (~16.2%) are core[3]". This total comes from the Eduardo et al. study in panel E, whose bars read 3155[4] core genes (>95%[5]), 7847[6] dispensable genes and 8467[7] unique genes. Added together, these come to 19,469[8], which matches the stated total exactly. The core share of that sum works out to 16.2[9]%, which also matches the stated percentage.

The other groups in panel E come from separate studies with different category definitions: Danesh et al. (core, soft core, shell, cloud) and Filipe et al. (core, accessory, unique). Their bars give different totals. The text does not give totals for them; it only says they[10] report broad genomic diversity. So they shouldn't be expected to add up to the stated total. Also, the bar values were read from the figure image by a vision model, not taken from printed text.

source.caption: Fig. 2. Phenotypic characteristics and genomic diversity of S. marcescens. (A) Temperature-dependent prodigiosin pigmentation phenotype; (B) distribution of the prodigiosin biosynthetic gene cluster among different biogroups; (C–D) GC content and genomic compositional characteristics; (E) pangenome composition and genomic variability; and (F) predicted host range of plasmids identified in S. marcescens. The figure summarizes the multi-level diversity of S. marcescens in phenotype, genome composition, and genetic plasticity.

source.text: In panel E, under the Eduardo et al. 2019 definition, the core genome (>95%) contains 3155 genes.

Fig. 2 is a composite six-panel figure describing Serratia marcescens phenotype and genomics, organized under two headers: a purple 'Pigmented phenotype' banner covering panels A and B, and a dark blue 'Genomic features' banner covering panels C–F. (A) A schematic with a thermometer and colour gradient bar (Low to High) shows a deeply pigmented agar plate with colonies at 25–28 °C versus a pale/nonpigmented plate at ≥37 °C. (B) A table combining the classification of David et al. 2022 (phylogeny, biotype, phenotype) with the percentage of isolates from each habitat (Grimont et al. 2006) for water (107 isolates), plants and rodents (37 isolates), and hospital patients (1066 isolates); L15 biotypes A1 and A2/6 are pigmented (red text), while L13/A3, L14/A4, L9/A5/8 and L12/TCT are nonpigmented. (C) A histogram with kernel density curve of genome GC content (%) with mean μ = 59.74% marked by a dashed vertical line; the distribution is left-skewed with a major peak near 60.0%. (D) A scatter plot with marginal density plots of coding GC (%) versus intergenic GC (%) with a fitted regression line, r = 0.57, p < 0.001. (E) A grouped bar chart of pangenome gene numbers under three definitions: Eduardo et al. 2019 (core >95% = 3155, dispensable = 7847, unique = 8467), Danesh et al. 2016 (core >99% = 3372, soft core 95–99% = 342, shell 15–95% = 1526, cloud <15% = 8347), and Filipe et al. 2018 (core 100% = 2107, accessory = 7656, unique = 6693). (F) A bar chart of plasmid proportion (%) by predicted host range: genus 23.9%, family 11.3%, order 30.2%, class 2.7%, phylum 9.0%, multi-phyla 22.9%.
